theory.intro: A **prime** number is a positive whole number with exactly two positive factors: $1$ and itself. A **composite** number is a positive whole number with more than two positive factors.
facts: $0$ and $1$ are **neither** prime nor composite; $2$ is the only even prime.
steps: For a positive whole number, count its distinct positive factors.
Exactly two factors → prime; more than two → composite.
$1$ has only one positive factor. $0$ is not a positive whole number. Both are neither prime nor composite.

workedExamples.question_text:
Classify each number as prime or composite. Show how you know.
(a) $47$
(b) $65$
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) Test factor pairs, as in finding all factors.
$47\div2=23$ remainder $1$.
$47\div3=15$ remainder $2$.
$47\div4=11$ remainder $3$.
$47\div5=9$ remainder $2$.
$47\div6=7$ remainder $5$.
$47\div7=6$ remainder $5$.
The possible partners have now passed each other, so there are no new pairs to test.
The only positive factors are $1$ and $47$. Therefore $47$ is prime.
(b) $5\times13=65$.
The positive factors are $1,5,13,65$. There are more than two, so $65$ is composite.

workedExamples.question_text: Classify (a) $0$, (b) $1$ and (c) $2$. Explain why being even does not always mean a number is composite.
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) $0$ is not a positive whole number, so it is neither prime nor composite.
(b) $1$ has just one positive factor, $1$, so it is neither.
(c) $2$ has exactly two positive factors, $1$ and $2$, so it is prime.
Although $2$ is even, it is prime. Every even number greater than $2$ has $2$ as a factor as well as $1$ and itself.

workedExamples.question_text:
(a) A number has the positive factors $1,3,17,51$. Classify it.
(b) A student says $25$ is prime because it is odd. Use a factor pair to correct the claim.
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a) There are four distinct positive factors, so the number is composite.
(b) $5\times5=25$.
The positive factors include $1,5,25$: three distinct factors. Do not count $5$ twice.
Therefore $25$ is composite, although it is odd.

workedExamples.question_text: Which number is prime: $19$, $27$, $35$ or $57$? Explain your choice.
workedExamples.solution_text:
$27=3\times9$, $35=5\times7$ and $57=3\times19$, so these are composite.
For $19$, testing $2$, $3$ and $4$ gives a remainder each time. At $5$, the partner is less than $5$, so there are no new pairs.
The only positive factors of $19$ are $1$ and $19$. Only $19$ is prime.

foundation.question_text: Classify $13$ as prime, composite or neither.
foundation.solution_text:
The factors of $13$ are $1$ and $13$.
It has exactly two factors, so $13$ is prime.

foundation.question_text: Classify $15$ as prime, composite or neither.
foundation.solution_text:
The factors of $15$ are $1,3,5,15$.
It has more than two factors, so $15$ is composite.

The factors of $2$ are $1$ and $2$.
It has exactly two factors, so $2$ is prime.

foundation.question_text: Classify $1$ as prime, composite or neither.
foundation.solution_text: $1$ has only one factor, so it is neither prime nor composite.

foundation.question_text: Classify $0$ as prime, composite or neither.
foundation.solution_text: $0$ is not a positive integer, so it is neither prime nor composite.

foundation.question_text: Classify $21$ as prime, composite or neither.
foundation.solution_text:
$3 \times 7=21$
So $21$ has factors other than $1$ and itself and is composite.

mastery.question_text: Without listing every factor, decide whether $91$ is prime or composite.
mastery.solution_text:

So $91$ has factors other than $1$ and itself and is composite.
